name: chusitoo/flatbush (C++ port of Flatbush)
workload: Packed Hilbert R-tree: index 1,000,000 rectangles, 1000 bounding-box searches at 10%/1%/0.01% area, k-nearest-neighbour searches (same cases as the JS bench.js).
claimed_speedup: C++ README table (i7-1185G7): index 1000000 rectangles 55ms (clang 18.1.3), 59ms (gcc 13.3.0), 72ms (cl 19.29); 1000 searches 10%: 79/80/91ms; 1 search of 1000000 neighbors: 88/86/63ms. JS original README (M1 Pro, Node v24): index 1,000,000 rectangles 109ms; 1 search of 1,000,000 neighbors 84ms. Ratio 109ms/55ms is about 2.0x for index build (derived from page data); the README itself makes no explicit speedup claim and the two tables use different CPUs. No comparison against Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS or nanoflann exists in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: clang 18.1.3, gcc 13.3.0, cl 19.29.30159; CMake WITH_BENCHMARKS sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release (explicit -O flags not stated); SSE2 default, AVX/AVX2/AVX512 selectable
hardware: Intel i7-1185G7 @ 3.00GHz, Win11 25H2 / Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS (C++ numbers); Apple M1 Pro, Node v24 (JS numbers at https://github.com/mourner/flatbush)
stars_or_usage: 25 stars; on Conan Center and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Static index: build once, no insert/delete after finish(). Header-only C++11, optional std::span, SIMD box tests, zero-copy fromView on aligned buffers, serialized layout compatible with the JS library.
caveats: No head-to-head against a baseline in the supplied baselines list (Boost.Geometry rtree, CGAL, GEOS) and none found in the repo or by one search. The only cross-implementation comparison is derived by reading two README tables measured on different CPUs and OSes (and the JS README table lists a different search mix), so it is directional. Author states benchmarks are based on the original bench to allow a close comparison. A search snippet of the project page shows older numbers (93ms clang 10.0.0), so the tables were rerun over time. Records the JS port as the incumbent; Boost.Geometry bulk-loaded R-tree comparisons are not documented.

name: Sobek (streaming equivariant tensor-product convolutions)
workload: Edge-conditioned equivariant tensor-product convolution (uvw and uvu operator families), forward, backward and double backward, on capacity-matched grids (16-profile UVW grid, 9-profile UVU grid); also peak memory.
claimed_speedup: Search snippet of arXiv 2607.18074 abstract: faster in all 75 capacity-matched comparisons across two operator families and all three differentiation orders, 1.2x to 49.7x, peak allocated memory reduced by up to 99%; at the last degree point shared with OpenEquivariance, OpenEquivariance allocates 24.1-27.1 GiB vs Sobek 0.1-0.4 GiB; runs workloads up to two orders of magnitude beyond OpenEquivariance capacity.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit 13.3 recommended (CUDA 12.9 builds about 25% slower per README); PyTorch >= 2.12 JIT extension builder; float32 with ieee or tf32 GEMMs; nvcc flags not stated
tradeoffs: CUDA/PyTorch only, float32 only; requires CUDA toolkit for JIT compile (first call per problem compiles specialised kernels). Supports uvw and homogeneous uvu contractions, fused radial projection so the caller must pass the compact radial embedding plus final projection weight. Deterministic, no atomics, bounded scratch (receiver_scratch_bytes).
caveats: The paper (arxiv.org) and mirrors were EGRESS_BLOCKED in this session, so the numbers are from WebSearch snippets of the abstract and could not be checked against tables; GPU model and per-case numbers unknown. Repo ships a benchmark CLI (suites minimal, scaling, throughput, uvu-throughput; 'matched' command for OpenEquivariance-capacity-matched timing) but the paper PDF is not in the repo (tree: sobek/, tests/, LICENSE, NOTICE, pyproject.toml). Preprint, not peer reviewed; authors are the repo owners (Cortex Discovery GmbH). Speedups are over a partly different formulation (Sobek fuses the radial projection while baselines take precomputed edge weights), and the comparison is capacity-matched against OpenEquivariance, so 1.2x-49.7x is a range over cases, not a typical figure. No evidence found of a Sobek benchmark against FlashTP in the paper snippets (README only lists FlashTP among related libraries). Oldest repo commit window is 2026-07-20 to 2026-07-24 (4 commits).

name: FlashTP (SNU-ARC)
baseline: e3nn o3.TensorProduct (uvu, with torch_scatter) and NVIDIA cuEquivariance
workload: Channelwise (uvu) tensor-product layer of equivariant MLIPs (NequIP, SevenNet-type irreps configs in ir_config/), kernel microbenchmarks and end-to-end SevenNet-l3i5 inference and training.
claimed_speedup: Search snippets of the ICML 2025 abstract: up to 41.6x and 60.8x kernel speedups over e3nn and NVIDIA cuEquivariance; SevenNet-l3i5 4.2x and 3.5x speedup with 6.3x and 6.2x peak-memory reduction for inference and training.
tradeoffs: Drop-in only for channelwise 'uvu' e3nn TensorProduct; CUDA 12+ and PyTorch >= 2.4.1; kernels compiled at install (up to 10 minutes), per-architecture (auto-detect, A100/H100 fallback with PTX); README TODO lists performance work and a JIT implementation.
caveats: Paper (openreview, proceedings.mlr.press) and arXiv were EGRESS_BLOCKED; numbers are from WebSearch snippets only, so GPU model, precision, compiler flags and the config on which 41.6x/60.8x peak occurs are unverified. Repo README gives no numbers; it ships microbenchmarks (example/test.sh runs flashTP_test.py on ir_config/nequip/4_32_3_p_sc.txt, fp32) that a user can rerun, so reproducibility is plausible but the stated hardware and flags are not in the repo page. The 'up to' figures are maxima. OpenEquivariance issue #171 (opened at https://github.com/PassionLab/OpenEquivariance/issues/171) contains a user remark that FlashTP seems to outperform cuEquivariance a lot at higher angular momentum, but states no numbers and notes the FlashTP authors did not benchmark against OpenEquivariance, so the lead that FlashTP wins at high l against OpenEquivariance is not supported. Sobek's README lists FlashTP as a related library but its snippets name only OpenEquivariance as the main baseline.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/SNU-ARC/flashTP README, WebSearch snippet of ICML 2025 paper, and https://github.com/PassionLab/OpenEquivariance/issues/171

name: CB-SpMV / CB-Sparse (xing-cong)
baseline: cuSPARSE BSR SpMV (cusparse_bsrmv, cuSPARSE v12.4); also TileSpMV and DASP
workload: FP64 SpMV Gflop/s averaged over 2,843 SuiteSparse matrices on A100 and RTX 4090, each kernel run 1000 times; cuSPARSE-BSR uses the best block size from 2x2, 4x4, 8x8 and 16x16.
claimed_speedup: Paper (ICS '25): over cuSPARSE-BSR average 2.95x (max 37.54x on TSOPF_FS_b39_c30) on RTX 4090 and 2.99x (max 54.27x on boyd1) on A100; over TileSpMV average 3.06x (max 8.56x on piston) on RTX 4090 and 3.95x (max 10.34x on rgg_n_2_21_s0) on A100; over DASP average 2.76x on RTX 4090 and 1.21x on A100. The abstract's 'up to 3.95x' is the A100 TileSpMV average.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper text (cuSPARSE v12.4 named as baseline); FP64 values, 16x16 sub-blocks
hardware: NVIDIA A100 (40 GB, 1.56 TB/s) and NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB, 1.01 TB/s); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: GPU-only (NVIDIA), needs conversion of CSR into the CB 2D block format (preprocessing cost, extra metadata); CPU-side aggregation of mixed-type data. Only CB-SpMV is released; CB-SpMM and CB-SpGEMM are 'coming soon (under review)'.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (ICS 2025) with code in the repo, but compiler, flags and host CPU are not stated, so B rather than A. The lead's snippet assigned 3.95x to A100 and 3.06x to RTX 4090 for TileSpMV and that matches the paper, but cuSPARSE-BSR is a blocked-format baseline (not cuSPARSE CSR), so the cuSPARSE number is against its BSR path with best-of-four block sizes. Averages are of per-matrix speedups. The advantage over DASP on A100 is only 1.21x. A recent commit (2026-09-02, 'bug fix and opt preprocess') postdates the paper, so numbers may differ from the current code. Not a CPU baseline: SuiteSparse, Eigen and PETSc are not compared.

name: Ocean SpGEMM (CornellHPC)
baseline: spECK (primary) and OpSparse; also TileSpGEMM and HSMU-SpGEMM
workload: GPU SpGEMM (C = A*B) on 337 square SuiteSparse matrices on A100, plus H100 and 64 rectangular matrices; replaces the symbolic pass with HyperLogLog estimation.
claimed_speedup: Search snippet of arXiv 2604.19004 abstract: on A100 over 337 square matrices Ocean achieves 1.4x, 2.6x, 3.5x and 2.0x over spECK, opSparse, TileSpGEMM and HSMU-SpGEMM; consistent speedup on H100 and 64 rectangular matrices; overall 1.4x-2.8x on A100 and H100.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit 12.4 or later; Makefile with sm_xx compute capability, NUM_SM and SHARED_MEMORY_KB set by hand (flags not stated in README)
hardware: NVIDIA A100 and H100 (tested only on these)
tradeoffs: Requires compute capability 8.0+ and CUDA 12.4+, manual hardware constants in include/Common.h, matrices must be converted to a custom .csr format with the bundled convert tool; README warns of likely compile or runtime errors on untested hardware. Part of the code is adapted from spECK; uses nlohmann/json and murmur3.
caveats: No LICENSE file and no license shown on the repo page, so usability is reference (code must not be copied); spECK origin of parts of the code adds licensing ambiguity. Paper (ICS 2026, doi 10.1145/3797905.3807868) is peer reviewed but arXiv, doi.org and alphaxiv were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the speedups are from WebSearch snippets and the cuSPARSE comparison, per-case numbers, CPU and flags could not be checked. The values '7.35x/1.43x/1.52x' in the lead are OpSparse's own reported averages over cuSPARSE, nsparse and spECK (OpSparse paper, arXiv 2206.07244), not Ocean results, and should not be attributed to Ocean. README says to use spECK output as ground truth and warns numerical comparison may fail on some matrices due to floating point error. No CPU baseline (SuiteSparse CPU, Eigen, PETSc) is compared.
